summary:
Egypt presents a direct and documented entry risk to trans visitors. The Ministry of Interior holds broad powers under the immigration law to refuse entry to, or deport, anyone whose presence is said to disturb public order and morality, and those powers have been applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Cairo 52 study "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" (27 November 2023) analyses that law and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents between 2018 and 2022. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights separately records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even where no charge is ever upheld. Removal therefore does not require any offence under Egyptian law.

Same-sex conduct is not expressly written into the penal statutes, but prosecutions are a routine outcome rather than a theoretical one. Economic Courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Article 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961, and Court of Cassation interpretations dating from the 1970s had already stripped out the requirement of a financial exchange, so habitual conduct or multiple partners is enough to sustain a charge. The cybercrime legislation adds six months' imprisonment and a fine for content held to violate "social and family values". The penalties that follow arrest are custodial.

Arrests are manufactured by police work rather than generated by complaints. The BBC investigation into how Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps describes officers running entrapment operations online, with victims recounting blackmail and detention, and the EIPR documentation identifies fake accounts used to draw in individuals, transgender women especially, on LGBTQ dating apps and websites. A visitor using those same apps is exposed to the same tactic. People taken into custody are subjected to coerced anal examinations, recorded by Bedayaa and by Human Rights Watch in its reporting on the Queen Boat-era crackdown, and the EIPR material notes violations continuing inside police stations after arrest.

Document handling at the border and in administrative dealings is tightening. A Ministry of Interior directive issued to civil-registry heads nationwide in December 2024 closes the Civil Status Law 143/1994 loophole that had allowed transgender people to correct their gender markers through governorate committees, which means corrected documents are increasingly difficult to obtain and mismatches between presentation and papers are more likely to be flagged.

Healthcare carries the same exposure. TIMEP's submission for Egypt's fourth Universal Periodic Review cycle (6 January 2025) finds discriminatory laws, policies and practices that violate the right to health for transgender and intersex people, pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in health services, and barriers to equitable care that persist since the preceding cycle. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity at its 2025 Universal Periodic Review.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement pattern has a long documented history. Human Rights Watch's report In a Time of Torture (29 February 2004) set out arbitrary arrests, beatings and confinement in dark cells on suspicion of homosexual conduct during the Queen Boat-era crackdown, with testimony from defendants, and the EIPR material on continuing violations inside police stations shows the same treatment logic still present two decades later.

Outright's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, states the gap plainly: homosexuality is not explicitly criminalised, yet vague public-morality and debauchery provisions are used to secure prison sentences. Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing adds that authorities turn a blind eye to harassment while arresting the people being harassed, and that Egypt maintains no anti-discrimination policy or law covering sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. The absence of any such statute removes the principal route to redress for a visitor who is stopped, searched or detained.
localsOnly:
For Egyptian residents, legal gender recognition has been actively foreclosed. The Civil Status Law 143/1994 had permitted correction of gender markers through governorate committees, and a Ministry of Interior directive distributed to civil-registry heads across the country in December 2024 was issued specifically to close that route.

Residents face the same health system described in TIMEP's January 2025 UPR submission: discriminatory laws, policies and practices, and widespread gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare that leaves transgender and intersex Egyptians without equitable access. Bedayaa's briefing documents rising arrests of homosexual and transgender people, deteriorating detention conditions, and the complete absence of anti-discrimination law or policy at national level.
outOfScopeNotes:
This inventory contains no source addressing restroom or facility access, nor any source describing how consular or border officers treat identity documents during routine screening; those questions remain unresolved here rather than answered negatively.

The 12 incidents analysed in "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" are reported as a set without individual outcomes, so the length of detentions and the number of deportations actually carried out are not established. The app-entrapment cases in the BBC reporting are anonymised at the victims' request, which leaves convictions and sentences unverifiable from this material.

The Ministry of Interior directive closing the gender-marker loophole is reported through civil-society documentation; whether a formal instrument has been published, and its exact text, is not confirmed in this inventory. The specific UN recommendations Egypt rejected at its 2025 Universal Periodic Review are cited in summary form here without the underlying session record.
